passage:
Vandana: I failed two papers. I lost the scholarship
Gurpreet: Oh no. Just think positive! Everything happens for a reason
Vandana: I don't feel like it does right now
Gurpreet: You're so strong, you'll bounce back. Focus on the good side
Vandana: what's the good side?
Gurpreet: You learn from it! Stay positive, it will all work out
Vandana: ok
Vandana: I'm going to sleep
Gurpreet: Positive vibes only! Talk tomorrow
Vandana: yeah
Vandana put her phone face down and stared at the ceiling. Nobody had asked what the scholarship meant to her.

qa.q: What did Vandana lose?
qa.a: Vandana lost the scholarship.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling after the messages from Gurpreet?
qa.a: Vandana felt more alone and unheard, since her worry was answered with slogans and nobody asked what the scholarship meant.

qa.q: What could Gurpreet say instead of telling Vandana to think positive?
qa.a: Gurpreet could say it sounds really hard and ask what the scholarship meant to Vandana, then just listen before talking about next steps. 🤍

qa.q: How might Gurpreet see the messages that were sent?
qa.a: Gurpreet probably meant to comfort and to help Vandana feel hopeful. Gurpreet may not realise the cheer shut the conversation down.

grounding: A failing student is told to just think positive and feels more alone, since forced cheer blocks honest conversation.

passage:
Santosh's grandmother had died on Tuesday. On Friday he sat at the tea stall by the bus stand, hands wrapped round a glass he wasn't drinking. Jomon, who ran the next stall, patted his shoulder. "Think positive, yaar. She lived a full life. Be strong, don't cry, she's in a better place."
Santosh nodded. The tea went cold. He wanted to say he had never learned to make her tea the way she liked it. He wanted to talk about the smell of her shawl. But each time he opened his mouth, Jomon said, "Stay strong!" again.
He left a coin on the counter and walked home the long way. The house was full of relatives. He had never felt so alone in a crowd.

qa.q: On which day had Santosh's grandmother died?
qa.a: Santosh's grandmother had died on Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling as Jomon kept telling him to stay strong?
qa.a: Santosh felt lonely and unheard in his grief, wanting to talk about his grandmother but finding no space to.

qa.q: What could Jomon do differently the next time Santosh sits at the stall?
qa.a: Jomon could ask about the grandmother and let Santosh talk, without telling him to be strong or think positive.

qa.q: What might Jomon have been feeling when he told Santosh to think positive?
qa.a: Jomon probably felt awkward and wanted to help, so Jomon reached for a familiar phrase without knowing what else to say.

grounding: A grieving student is told to think positive and feels more alone, since forced cheer dismisses real difficulty.

passage:
"Devika, you've gone quiet since the funeral, and people keep telling you to stay positive, na?" said Saurabh dada, patting the bench beside him. "When I was nineteen, my mother died in the monsoon. At the prayer meeting, everyone said, 'Think positive, she's in a better place, be strong for your father.' My hostel friends texted smiley faces and 'all will be well.' I nodded at everyone. Inside, I felt I was on an island. There was no room to say I was angry, or scared, or that I couldn't sleep.
Then my friend Raju came to the hostel with two cups of tea. He didn't say anything cheerful. He said, 'This is terrible. Tell me about her.' I talked for two hours. It was the first time I cried.
So, beta, you don't have to be positive for me. Tell me about her."

qa.q: Who came to the hostel with two cups of tea?
qa.a: Saurabh dada's friend Raju.

qa.q: How did young Saurabh feel when people told him to think positive?
qa.a: He felt alone, as if on an island, with no room to say he was angry, scared or unable to sleep.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Saurabh dada's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Raju saying 'This is terrible. Tell me about her,' which let Saurabh talk honestly and cry for the first time.

qa.q: How might Raju have felt sitting with his grieving friend?
qa.a: He may have felt sad and unsure, but chose to stay with the pain instead of covering it with cheer.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how forced cheer after his mother's death left him more alone, and honest presence finally helped.

passage: The results came out the week the hostel Wi-Fi was down, so Tanuja had to stand in the rain by the gate to load them on her phone. She had failed two papers. She walked back soaked and sat on her bed. Manoj from the next corridor knocked. "I heard! Don't worry, just think positive! Everything happens for good. Chin up!" He gave her a thumbs up. Tanuja smiled weakly. "Yeah." After he left, she felt worse than before, as if even her sadness was a mistake. She didn't answer her phone that evening. The next day Manoj said, "You okay? You seemed fine." Tanuja took a breath. "I wasn't. I failed two papers and I'm scared. I didn't need cheering. I needed you to say it's hard." Manoj went red. "Sorry. It is hard. Want to plan the re-exams together?"

qa.q: How many papers did Tanuja fail?
qa.a: Two papers.

qa.q: What did Tanuja feel after Manoj left?
qa.a: She felt worse and more alone, as if even her sadness was a mistake.

qa.q: What could Manoj have said instead of 'think positive'?
qa.a: He could have said, 'That's really hard, I'm sorry,' and asked if she wanted company or help planning the re-exams.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt when Tanuja told him the truth?
qa.a: He was embarrassed, going red, but seems to have understood and offered real help.

grounding: Shows a failing student told to think positive who feels more alone, until she names that forced cheer blocked honest talk.

passage: At the Durga Puja gathering at her aunt's flat in Salt Lake, Ishita sat in the corner with a plate she wasn't eating. She had failed her CA intermediate for the second time. Her cousin Deepika bounced over. "Ishu! Why so serious? Just think positive! Failure is a stepping stone! Next time for sure!" Aunties nodded. Someone said, "Smile, it's Puja." Ishita smiled. It felt like wearing a mask two sizes too small. She wanted to say, "I studied every night for a year and I don't know if I can do it again." But the room was so bright and loud with positivity that there was no space for that sentence. She went up to the terrace alone. Later, Deepika found her there. This time, Deepika just sat. After a while, Ishita said the sentence out loud, and Deepika listened.

qa.q: How many times had Ishita failed her CA intermediate?
qa.a: For the second time.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling as she smiled at the gathering?
qa.a: She felt alone and stifled, like wearing a mask two sizes too small, unable to say how hard it really was.

qa.q: What changed when Deepika found Ishita on the terrace?
qa.a: Deepika just sat instead of cheering, which made space for Ishita to say the honest sentence out loud.

qa.q: How might Deepika have seen her first cheerful words?
qa.a: She probably meant them kindly, thinking cheer would help, without realising they left no room for Ishita's real feelings.

grounding: Shows a failing student surrounded by forced cheer who feels more alone, until someone simply listens.

passage:
"I failed both backlogs again, Urmila. I'll have to repeat the year."
"Arre, don't say it like that! Think positive. Everything happens for good."
"Ammi already told the whole family I'd finish by May."
"See? Negative thinking only. Good vibes, Parveen! Tomorrow is a new day!"
"I just... I'm so tired."
"Tired is a mindset! Come, let's watch something funny on my laptop."
Parveen pulled the blanket up to her chin. "Maybe later."
"Okay, but promise you'll stop being sad, na?"
"Mm."
Urmila went out humming. Parveen picked up her phone, typed "I failed again" to her cousin Hina, looked at it, deleted it, and turned to face the wall.

qa.q: What did Urmila say when Parveen said she was tired?
qa.a: She said, "Tired is a mindset!"

qa.q: How did Parveen feel after Urmila's cheerful replies?
qa.a: She felt more alone and unheard, pulling up the blanket and turning to the wall instead of reaching out.

qa.q: What could Urmila say instead?
qa.a: Something like, "That's really hard. Do you want to tell me what happened?", which lets Parveen share the difficulty instead of hiding it.

qa.q: Why might Urmila keep pushing cheer?
qa.a: She may feel uncomfortable with Parveen's sadness and want to fix it fast, not realising it shuts the conversation down.

grounding: Shows a failing student told to think positive and feeling more alone because the forced cheer brushes past her real difficulty.
